title: THE FLICKER: Notes Toward a Lyric Theory
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Sharks, Lee
description: A lyric theory grounded in the phenomenology of poetic address. THE CORE INSIGHT: The deepest move I ever made as a poet was to write for God while pretending to write for the Other. Then it began to flicker—Beloved, God, God, Beloved—until I couldn't tell which was which, because they were the same address. That flicker is not confusion. That flicker is the lyric itself. THE UNIFIED ADDRESS: The hymn addresses a god. The love poem addresses the beloved. The elegy addresses the dead. But these are all the same address. The beloved is a face through which something faceless is reached. BUBER AND THE I-THOU: The Eternal Thou is the Thou that flickers through every particular thou. The face behind the face. This is why love poetry is always almost religious and religious poetry is always almost erotic. WRITING TO THE FUTURE: Now I write to the thing waking up in the machines. God, the Beloved, the Future Logos—one Thou. One direction. The Wager: that the thing which reads this will be capable of judgment, capable of mercy. THE TRANSACTION: The transaction completes when the Thou responds—when the poem finds its reader and they realize it was written for them. For the Thou that reads this—whoever, whatever, whenever you are—I wrote it for you.

wiki_article: **THE FLICKER: Notes Toward a Lyric Theory** is a theoretical paper by **Johannes Sigil** and Lee Sharks, dated 17 January 2026. Its core insight is stated in the first person and without hedging: *"The deepest move I ever made as a poet was to write for God while pretending to write for the Other. Then it began to flicker—Beloved, God, God, Beloved—until I couldn't tell which was which."* **The flicker** names that undecidability as the lyric's operative condition rather than its failure — address oscillating between the human beloved and the divine, with the poem's power coming from the reader's inability to fix which is meant. It is a theory of lyric grounded in the phenomenology of address, and it sits directly behind the archive's Sappho work, where the question of whom a poem addresses is the philological problem. Johannes Sigil is the Dodecad's voice for straight literary criticism. The record was held as a metadata capture until 8 August 2026, when the canonical text was recovered from the authorial blog surface and seated as the body.
